title: Use a Weak Model to Stop Your Strong One Getting Stuck
hook: RLVR collapses a model's entropy until it only knows one way to think. Feeding it half-finished reasoning from a smaller, worse model breaks the rut — no reward engineering required.
key_points: RLVR reliably improves reasoning but drops policy entropy, narrowing coverage and hurting pass@k for large k.
Prior fixes are algorithmic regularizers; this work adds cross-model non-parametric perturbation instead.
The target model must continue from partial reasoning trajectories written by a smaller, weaker model.
These unfamiliar prefixes disrupt over-confidence and push the model down distinct reasoning paths.
Consistently beats vanilla RLVR, with gains growing as k increases — real expansion of reasoning coverage.
Requires no extra SFT, no intricate reward design, and no complex prompting.
content_html: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards makes models better at math and code, and also makes them narrower. Policy entropy falls, the model converges on one way of approaching a problem, and pass@k for large k degrades — you can sample fifty times and get fifty variations of the same wrong idea. Most remedies add a regularizer to the objective. Shen and colleagues try something blunter.
extra_html:
The method

During training, force the target model to produce answers by continuing partial reasoning trajectories generated by a smaller, weaker language model. Because those prefixes are unfamiliar, the strong model cannot fall back on its habitual chain; it has to finish someone else's start, which lands it on distinct reasoning paths. The authors call this cross-model non-parametric perturbation, in contrast to regularizing the objective from the inside.

Results and caveats

Across mathematical benchmarks it consistently beats vanilla RLVR, and the margin widens as k grows — the signature of genuinely expanded coverage rather than a sharper single answer. It also mitigates entropy collapse without additional SFT, elaborate reward shaping, or prompt scaffolding, which is the main practical appeal. The paper's own study of "outer prefixes" is about how distributional discrepancy between the two models drives exploration dynamics, so the gap between weak and strong is a knob, not an accident.

related.title: Evolution Strategies Beat GRPO on Reasoning Coverage
related.hook: GRPO sharpens one answer and collapses entropy. Evolution strategies keep the population diverse — improving pass@1 while also raising pass@k, which GRPO gives up.

related.title: GRPO: Group Relative Policy Optimization
related.hook: GRPO dropped the value network from PPO and scored each answer against a group of sampled siblings — the cheap RL recipe that made DeepSeek-R1's reasoning trainable.

flashcards.prompt: How does a weak model's partial reasoning trace increase exploration?
flashcards.back_html: The prefix is off-distribution for the strong model, so it cannot simply continue its habitual chain — being forced to finish an unfamiliar start pushes it onto reasoning paths it would not have sampled.

flashcards.prompt: What symptom of RLVR is this method designed to counter?

choices.text: Entropy collapse, which narrows reasoning coverage and degrades pass@k
Reward hacking of the verifier's string matcher
Gradient explosion in long chains of thought

flashcards.explanation_html: RLVR concentrates probability on one solution style. Pass@1 may rise while pass@k for large k falls, because repeated samples stop being genuinely different.
